title: Hand-off: poll, commands, readiness and status

story: Monday, 09:00. You assign RH-1234 to Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent: the empty projects table should show a "No projects yet" card. Two minutes later a teammate assigns RH-1301 to Nova as well. Its whole description is one line: "Make the projects page better."

Imagine Nova treated both tickets the same way. For RH-1301 it would claim a machine, read the code for an hour and post a plan built on guesses: faster loading, maybe, or a new layout. Your teammate would read it and answer "no, I meant the filters", and the hour and the machine would be gone. Somebody has to notice that RH-1301 is not a job yet, and the cheapest moment to notice is before any machine starts.
hook.question: How does Nova decide, in seconds and before it pays for a machine, whether a ticket is clear enough to start?

p: Three things happen between your click in Jira and the first machine. First, the Jira poll, a small scheduled job that asks Jira every minute which tickets are assigned to Nova, finds RH-1234 and reads its changelog to learn who assigned it. That person, you, becomes the requester: the one person who may approve Nova's plan, and the one person who may never approve its pull request. Second, the poll starts one Temporal run for the ticket, named nova:RH-1234, so the next poll a minute later joins that run instead of starting another one. You built both of these in the lessons on Jira and on Temporal.

The third thing is the subject of this lesson. The first step of the run is a readiness check: one model call that reads the ticket text and gives a verdict, a fixed answer the workflow can branch on. There are three verdicts: ready, ask, and hand back. The call runs on the orchestrator with Sonnet at low effort, not on a VM, so it costs a few cents and takes a few seconds. Finding the same thing out on a VM costs a machine for an hour and a plan that nobody can approve.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what people see during the hand-off
p: People should be able to follow a ticket without opening Slack, and without a new Jira comment every few minutes. So each ticket gets exactly one Nova comment. The first status update creates it, the workflow keeps its ID, and every later update edits the same comment in place. A single-select field called Nova state shows the same thing for boards and filters: Checking, Planning, Awaiting approval, Working and PR open, with Needs info and Stopped as side exits. Only the three states that need a person (Awaiting approval, Needs info and PR open) notify anybody; the rest are silent edits.

People also talk to Nova in the places they already use. A Jira comment that mentions Nova and starts with a command word, such as "@Nova stop", becomes a signal to the run, and a plain reply that mentions Nova counts as an answer to its open question. Jira stores comments as a JSON tree, so the code looks for a mention node with Nova's account ID instead of searching the text, and a quoted "@Nova" cannot fool it. Taking the ticket away from Nova counts as Stop too. And a person always owns the ticket: Nova assigns it back to the requester when its PR is marked ready, or when the run stops or hands back.

read.h: A verdict with reasons, not just a yes or no
p: The check reads the summary, the description, the comments and the titles of linked tickets. It never reads attachments or images. Screenshots and pasted logs are where real customer data and PHI hide (PHI is protected health information, the patient data our product holds), and no model call of ours may see it. For the same reason, when the text itself looks like it holds real patient data, the verdict is hand back and nothing goes further.

The answer is structured output, the JSON-that-must-match-a-schema you met in the lesson on judges. Each field is there because a later step needs it. The verdict picks the branch. The reason is one sentence the requester reads if the ticket comes back. The size (small, bigger or fuzzy) decides whether Nova asks questions before it plans. how_to_check says how a person could see that the change works, and an empty how_to_check is a strong sign that the ticket is not ready, because a change that nobody can check cannot be proved. questions holds at most five specific questions, and out_of_scope flags areas that are outside the pilot. The kind (a frontend bug, a backend bug, new tests and so on) is not used to decide anything here; it is kept so that later measurements can be split by kind of work.

notes.text: The branch. Every later step of the workflow starts from this one value.
bigger tickets get questions first; fuzzy ones also get several plans and a judge (later lessons).
Empty means the model sees no way to check the change. Treat it as a warning.
At most five, each answerable in one line. A model that writes six fails the parse.
Always draft-7: the SDK validates JSON Schema draft-07 and refuses the draft 2020-12 that zod writes by default.

read.see:
{
  "verdict": "ready",
  "reason": "One screen state with a clear text, in one area of the frontend.",
  "kind": "fe_bug",
  "size": "small",
  "how_to_check": "Open a workgroup with no projects and read the card.",
  "questions": [],
  "out_of_scope": []
}

p: Now the workflow branches. Ready means Nova starts planning. Ask means the questions go to the requester, in a Jira comment that mentions them and in the ticket's Slack thread, and the run waits for the answer without holding any machine; that waiting step is called the grill, and the next lesson builds it. A ticket that is ready but bigger than small gets its open questions first as well, because a five-minute answer is cheaper than a plan built on a guess. Hand back means Nova assigns the ticket back to the requester with the reason as a comment, and the run ends.

Hand back is for tickets that cannot be done as written, not for tickets that need one more sentence. A ticket that hides two changes in one, a ticket with real data in it, or a ticket in an area the pilot leaves out goes back. The pilot scope is a short list of areas people chose to keep out while we learn: database migrations, login code, the contract between our cloud and the on-premises client, and the CI files. It is a choice, not a wall. The readiness check flags these areas from the text, and if an edit lands in one of them later in the run, Nova stops and asks instead of continuing on its own.

notes.text: An activity: one Sonnet call with no tools and no repo. If it returns no usable verdict it throws, and Temporal retries it.
Assign the ticket back with the reason as a comment. The run ends here, before any machine.
ask, or ready but bigger: post the questions and wait for the requester. The next lesson.
Only now does a machine start, and a small one: plans are written on a lite VM.

read.h: Measure it before you trust it
p: The readiness check is a model, so it will sometimes be wrong. Before it is switched on, people label 30 past tickets by hand as ready, ask or hand back, and the same tickets go through the check. Then you compare the two in a confusion matrix: a small table with the person's label in the rows and the model's verdict in the columns. The diagonal is where they agree. Every other cell is one particular kind of mistake, and that is the useful part, because the kinds do not cost the same.

Look at the ready column first. A ticket the person called ask but the model called ready means a plan built on guesses and a machine for an hour. A ticket the person handed back but the model called ready is the worst cell, because Nova goes to work on something that should never have started. The other mistakes are cheap: an ask for a ticket that was ready costs the requester one extra question. So the rule for switching the check on is not only a high agreement number. It is also zero tickets in the dangerous cells, which we call false readies. Below is the table from the lab: ten agreements out of twelve, and one false ready, a ticket that renames an API field and migrates old rows.
read.see:
person ↓  model →   ready     ask       hand_back
ready               4         1         0
ask                 0         4         0
hand_back           1         0         2

lab.title: Is the readiness check good enough to switch on?
needs: About 20 MB of disk for zod and tsx
lab.goal: Turn a readiness verdict into the next step, then compare recorded verdicts with hand labels in a confusion matrix and decide whether the check may be switched on.

guess.q: Out of 12 past tickets, the model agrees with the person on 10. The two mistakes: it asked a question about a ticket the person called ready, and it called ready a ticket the person handed back. Should the check be switched on?

options.text: Yes, 83% agreement is good for a model.
options.why: The number hides which mistakes happened. One of the two is the most expensive kind there is.

options.text: No: one ticket that should have gone back would have started real work.
options.why: A false ready means a machine and a plan for a ticket that should never have started. That one cell blocks it, whatever the agreement number says.

options.text: No: the extra question about a ready ticket is the problem.
options.why: That mistake costs the requester one answer. It is annoying, but cheap.

check.q: Why does Nova check a ticket's readiness before it claims any VM?

options.text: Because the VM cannot reach Jira, so the ticket must be read first
options.why: A VM can read its own ticket through the broker. The reason is cost, not access.

options.text: Because a few cents and a few seconds now can save a machine-hour and a plan nobody can approve
options.why: The check needs only the ticket text, so it runs without a machine. Stopping a fuzzy ticket here is the cheapest stop in the whole run.

options.text: Because the model is not allowed to read code before a person approves
options.why: Nova reads code while it plans, before any approval. The readiness check simply does not need code.

check.q: A ticket's description contains rows pasted from a real customer's patient list, with names. What does the readiness check answer?

options.text: ask, with a question about which row is wrong
options.why: Asking would keep the run going with real patient data in its input. Real data stops the run.

options.text: ready, because the bug is described clearly
options.why: Clear or not, no model call of ours may work on real patient data.

options.text: hand back, with the reason, and nothing goes further
options.why: When the text looks like it holds real patient data, the ticket goes back to the requester and no machine ever sees it.

check.q: You compare the check with 30 hand-labelled tickets. Which result alone is enough to keep it switched off?

options.text: One ticket a person called hand back that the model called ready
options.why: That is a false ready: real work would start on a ticket that should never have started. The rule is zero of those.

options.text: Three tickets a person called ready that the model wanted to ask about
options.why: Each one costs the requester an extra answer. Worth improving, but cheap.
The percentage alone does not say which mistakes happened. You need the matrix to see whether any are dangerous.

p: The hand-off is four pieces in the orchestrator. Nova's entry in the registry of Jira queries becomes the poll-jira-nova schedule: every minute, as the Nova Atlassian service account, with a scoped API token from Vault (infrastructure/ai-agents/jira-nova) that only the orchestrator workers get. requesterOf takes the requester from the nova.requester issue property that /nova RH-1234 sets in Slack, or else from the latest changelog entry that assigned the ticket to Nova; it must ignore changes made by Nova's own account, or a reassignment through /nova could make Nova its own requester. commands.ts reads @Nova start, answer, retry, stop, approve and change from the comment's ADF tree, and the poller sends each one as a signal to open runs.

checkReadiness is the first activity of ticketToPr: Sonnet 5.5 at low effort, no tools, settingSources [], the prompt in orchestrator/prompts/readiness.md with 6 to 8 labelled examples, and PILOT_EXCLUDED listing the migration, auth, gRPC contract and infra paths. The ticket's sketch converts the schema with z.toJSONSchema(Readiness); it needs { target: "draft-7" }. Before it is switched on, 30 past RH tickets are labelled by hand and compared. setStatus keeps one comment per ticket and the Nova state custom field, whose ID lives in jira-fields.ts once a Jira admin creates it.

tickets.why: The Nova service account, the one-minute poll and the requester from the changelog.
@Nova commands, /nova in Slack, unassign as stop, and giving the ticket back.
The readiness check itself: the schema, the three verdicts, the pilot scope and the hand-labelled comparison.
One status comment edited in place and the Nova state field.

words.plain: One cheap model call, before any machine, that reads the ticket text and says whether Nova can start.
The fixed answer the workflow branches on: ready, ask or hand back.
Nova assigns the ticket back to the requester with a reason, and the run ends.
Areas people chose to keep out while Nova is new: migrations, login, the client contract, CI files.
Protected health information: real patient data. It never goes into a prompt.
A table of the person's labels against the model's answers; each cell off the diagonal is one kind of mistake.

review.q: From memory: the three verdicts, and what the workflow does after each one.
review.a: ready: plan on a lite VM (a bigger ticket asks its questions first). ask: post the questions to the requester in Jira and Slack and wait with no machine. hand back: assign the ticket back with the reason and end the run.

review.q: A teammate wants the readiness check to read attachments "so it sees the screenshots too". What do you answer?
review.a: Attachments and screenshots are where real customer or patient data hides, and no prompt may contain it. The check reads the summary, description, comments and linked titles only; if the text itself looks like real data, it hands the ticket back.

review.q: Which cell of the confusion matrix decides whether the check may be switched on, and why that one?
review.a: Model ready while the person said ask or hand back: a false ready. It starts a machine and a plan for a ticket that should not start, which is the most expensive mistake. The rule is zero false readies plus high agreement.

remember: Before any machine starts, one cheap call reads the ticket and says ready, ask or hand back; trust it only after you have counted its false readies.
